import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The Goormaghtigh conjecture

A repunit is a number whose digits in some base are all $1$. Here a nontrivial representation has
at least three digits. The Goormaghtigh conjecture says that $31$ and $8191$ are the only numbers
having nontrivial repunit representations in two different bases.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goormaghtigh_conjecture)
* J. Grantham,
  [No new Goormaghtigh primes up to $10^{700}$](https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/y98/y98.pdf)
-/

namespace Goormaghtigh

/-- The repunit with `digits` digits in the given base, expressed without division. -/
def repunit (base digits : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ∑ i ∈ Finset.range digits, base ^ i

/-- A number having repunit representations of at least three digits in two distinct bases. -/
def IsGoormaghtighNumber (N : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ base₁ base₂ digits₁ digits₂ : ℕ,
    2 ≤ base₁ ∧ 2 ≤ base₂ ∧ base₁ ≠ base₂ ∧
      3 ≤ digits₁ ∧ 3 ≤ digits₂ ∧
        repunit base₁ digits₁ = N ∧ repunit base₂ digits₂ = N

/-- The only Goormaghtigh numbers are $31$ and $8191$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem goormaghtigh_conjecture (N : ℕ) (hN : IsGoormaghtighNumber N) :
    N = 31 ∨ N = 8191 := by
  sorry

/-- The number $31$ is a repunit in bases $2$ and $5$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isGoormaghtighNumber_31 : IsGoormaghtighNumber 31 := by
  refine ⟨2, 5, 5, 3, ?_⟩
  norm_num [repunit]

/-- The number $8191$ is a repunit in bases $2$ and $90$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isGoormaghtighNumber_8191 : IsGoormaghtighNumber 8191 := by
  refine ⟨2, 90, 13, 3, ?_⟩
  norm_num [repunit]

/-- Allowing two-digit repunits would make $13$ a representation in two distinct bases. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem repunit_two_digits : repunit 3 3 = 13 ∧ repunit 12 2 = 13 := by
  norm_num [repunit]

end Goormaghtigh

reformulations.difference: Lean classifies the common value N using finite geometric sums and unordered, distinct bases, rather than directly classifying the ordered equation solutions with x > y > 1 and n > m > 2.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For base ≥ 2, repunit base digits equals (base^digits − 1)/(base − 1), including as an exact rational quotient. The distinct bases can be reordered so x > y; strict increase in the base and monotonicity in the digit count then force m < n. The only permitted representations of 31 are (base,digits) = (2,5),(5,3), and those of 8191 are (2,13),(90,3). These representation classifications were proved using bounds base ≤ 90 and digits ≤ 13 followed by a finite decide check. Thus classifying N is equivalent to classifying the source’s two ordered quadruples. The full equivalence is proved independently in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean as Review.conjecture_equivalence, without using the conjecture’s sorry.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goormaghtigh_conjecture — lead, representation sections, partial results, and references (rendered revision 1350923251).
J. Grantham, No new Goormaghtigh primes up to 10^700, Integers 24 (2024), #A98, pp. 1–4: https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/y98/y98.pdf
review.notes: Checked all six declarations. Evaluations confirmed the empty and small-input behavior, both known witnesses, and the two-digit example for 13. Also proved independently that IsGoormaghtighNumber N implies 31 ≤ N. The three existing test proofs and the equivalence/boundary proofs have no sorryAx dependency. Both references retain the general conjecture as open; Grantham’s prime search is only a partial result. Grantham’s displayed Conjecture 1 contains an apparent ordering typo (y > x together with n > m); its abstract/introduction and Wikipedia’s explicit repunit formulation unambiguously support the Lean statement.
